cells.tense: Something carried here has reached its end and holds on its own, and the one who carried it knows the work is theirs.
cells.ask: Start one continuing thing here and say whose it is — the next version of the shared table, its opener said out loud.
cells.core:
Something in what gets shared here is done. A way of doing things that stuck, a phrase people kept, something carried until it could stand without help — and you know you carried it. That's why it holds. You didn't inherit it by accident and you don't have to defend it.

A shelf of this kind is rarely full, and the next piece is yours to start. Add one continuing thing and say out loud whose it is — the next version of the shared table, its first move said by you. What that gives back is something people can reach for and find, not just watch.

cells.tense: The ending is still ahead in the person's mind, and the person is gripping it so it can't be taken away.
cells.ask: Point at one finished thing here, leave it alone tomorrow, and let the next answer come from whoever is actually involved.
cells.core:
A shared way of doing things works best when it's already carried and can be left alone — a custom people keep without anyone standing over it, a phrase that survives on its own. That's the easy version, and it's real.

The hard version is you guarding an ending that hasn't arrived. What needs finishing gets picked up again and held tighter, checked twice, the ending rehearsed before it's real — and the grip is showing. People around the table can feel the squeeze before anyone says anything. Let the next answer come from where things are: pick one finished thing here and leave it be tomorrow, and let the person involved say the next line instead of you. That hands back the thing that holds up once you've stopped holding it, and the room still saying it.

cells.tense: A door closed back there, and the person is still standing at it, not turning around.
cells.ask: Pick one thing already carried here and say out loud what it needs next, then wait a day before answering.
cells.core:
You're standing at a door that closed behind you. Something got built here once, or tried to, and the turning-around didn't happen — so this side of life stays still while the rest keeps moving. Others arrange themselves around the stillness and hear what isn't chosen.

The way back in is smaller than it looks. Pick one thing already carried here — a habit, a phrase, a way of doing things — and say out loud what it needs next. Then wait a day before answering. That gives back the floor under a lot of feet learning that what gets passed on can still be chosen. The choice is yours to give it again.

cells.tense: What's shared here is already being made, and the person is doing it without noticing their own hand in it.
cells.ask: Name one custom you started or kept going and say 'I put that there' with no one else in the sentence.
cells.core:
When this is working, it looks like a kitchen people drift into without being asked — a phrase that keeps getting repeated, a season that keeps getting kept, a way of doing things that holds because someone kept doing it. You're one of the ones doing the keeping, most days without flagging it.

That's what makes it hard to see. The custom feels like how things are, not like something added. Say the hand once: pick one custom you started or kept alive and own it — one sentence, 'I put that there,' no one else in the sentence. That opens the real inheritance: the next shared habit gets chosen, not just picked up.

attempts.check: The unsupported personal claim I'm tempted by is 'you built this and it's still standing' — the record says a material cycle has reached completion, which holds for anything a person has made and finished, so I keep it modest and let the reader say no. A reasonable reader might hear the Unacknowledged cell as denying that anyone else helped, which is why the ask is about one thing they repeated, not about credit; the Too Little cell might sound like it demands a project when the person has no room, so the act is pointing at one existing thing, not starting anything. The ask survives being wrong: pointing at one thing, waiting a day for an answer, saying 'I put that there' — each teaches the person something about their own hand even if I've misread their season. The sentence that served the writer rather than the reader was an early 'you were making it the whole time' — it argued instead of described, so it's gone.
